I almost didn't go to Albania. Then I got lost on a Tuesday afternoon in Vlore, followed my nose, and ate the best pizza of my life in a place with no English menu and zero TripAdvisor reviews.

I almost didn't go to Albania.

That's the thing nobody tells you about travel — half the best moments in your life happen because of a last-minute decision that made zero logical sense. I'd been bouncing around Europe, doing the usual thing, hitting the spots that show up first when you Google "where to go in the Balkans." And then someone — I still can't remember who — said "have you been to Vlore?"

I hadn't. I barely knew where it was.

Three months later, I had an apartment there.

But let me back up, because the story that matters — the one that still makes me laugh when I think about it — is about a pizza place. A specific pizza place. One I only found because I got completely lost on a Tuesday afternoon with no plan, no Google Maps signal, and a stubborn refusal to ask for directions.

Vlore is a coastal city in southern Albania that most tourists completely skip. They go to Saranda, maybe Himara, maybe they do the Blue Eye and call it a day. Vlore is where actual Albanians live, work, and spend their summers. That was exactly why I stayed.

I'd been walking for about an hour — the kind of aimless walking where you're technically exploring but really you're just refusing to admit you have no idea where you are — when I turned a corner and smelled something. Pizza. Real pizza. Coming from a place with no English sign, no tourist photos in the window, no menu posted outside.

The kind of place that either kills you or becomes your favorite restaurant in the world.

I went in.

## How to Find the Good Neighborhoods

There's no algorithm for this. The best I can offer:

Walk further than feels comfortable. The tourist radius around most landmarks is about a ten-minute walk in any direction. Go twenty minutes. Go thirty. The neighborhood changes.

Eat breakfast somewhere. Breakfast spots attract locals more reliably than dinner spots — tourists are usually still recovering from the night before, and the locals are getting their day started. Watch where people walk. Walk that way.

Ask your accommodation host, not for "the best restaurant" (they'll tell you what tourists want to hear) but for where they go on a Sunday afternoon with their family. That's the question that gets you real answers.

This isn't a contrarian stance — it's a practical one. The tourist areas are usually the worst version of a place, and once you understand why, you can't unsee it.

Let me tell you about the worst meal I've ever had while traveling.

It was in [ADD YOUR DETAILS: the city — somewhere with a famous tourist area]. I was tired, I was hungry, and the restaurant was right there, on the main square, with photos of the food in the window and a guy outside telling me I'd made an excellent choice by stopping. The menu had English, German, French, and Spanish translations. The food arrived in about four minutes.

It was bad. Not "this is different from what I expected" bad. Just bad. Generic, overpriced, made for a customer who would never come back.

That customer was me.

I paid it, walked around the corner, and found a place with no tourist menu, no English signs, and a line of locals waiting for a table. I came back the next day for the same thing.

That's the whole story. That's also the entire argument.

## Why Tourist Areas Exist (And Why They're a Trap)

Tourist areas exist because travel became an industry. And like any industry, it optimized for efficiency — for getting the most money from the most people in the least amount of time with the least friction.

That means restaurants that can turn tables fast. Shops selling the same keychains you'll find in every city in the country. Bars that know exactly what a tourist wants and deliver it at a tourist price.

None of this is evil. It's just not real.

The real city — the one where people actually live — is always close. Usually within walking distance. Almost always more interesting.

---

## What "Tourist Area" Actually Means

It's not about being off the beaten path. It's about being honest about what you're looking at.

A tourist area is any place that has primarily optimized for visitors rather than residents. That can be a neighborhood, a street, a specific block, or even a single restaurant surrounded by good ones. The signs are usually the same:

Menus with photos. Aggressive hospitality from someone standing outside. Prices that are noticeably higher than the surrounding area. An absence of locals actually eating or drinking there.

## When Tourist Areas Are Actually Fine

I'm not a purist. There are times when the tourist area is right.

When you're exhausted and just need to eat something without an adventure. When you're somewhere for 12 hours and don't have time to explore. When you're with people who need the menu in English because they're new to travel and this isn't the moment to push them out of their comfort zone.

## The Actual Point

Travel is not a highlight reel. The best moments I've had — the conversations, the meals, the places that permanently changed something in how I see the world — have never happened in places that were built for me to have them.

They happen in the margins. In the neighborhoods. In the restaurants you walk past twice before deciding the plastic chairs are actually a good sign. In the conversations that start because you're genuinely lost, not performing being lost for a photo.

Skip the tourist area. Turn left instead of right. See what's at the end of the street.

That's where the trip actually is.

Hey, I'm Ubaldo — but you can call me Baldo. A California boy, 22 countries, a hotel room in Scotland, and a one-way ticket to Mexico. This is where it starts.

Hiya,

I'm Ubaldo but you can call me Baldo or Ubi (my nickname on the Hilltown). And yes, I'm always somewhere but home, mostly because I no longer have one.

I was born and raised in the Central Coast of California, the son of a Mexican family, which means I grew up living between two worlds before I ever boarded a plane. That perspective of seeing things from the outside in turned out to be the greatest tool I ever had. If you've ever felt like you didn't quite belong where you were, you're going to fit in here just fine.

For a long time I stayed put. Low confidence, crooked teeth, and a quiet depression that kept me rooted in a place that never quite felt like enough. Then I got braces. A few weeks in I noticed a change. Felt a bit better about myself and decided to book a trip to Jamaica with a friend. The day they came off, I barely recognized myself and things changed quickly. My first move? A group trip to Colombia. Just like that, Baldo was born.

Since then I've lived in California, Scotland, and Mexico, spent a few months in Albania, a month in New York (Queens), and chunks of time in places like Fargo, ND. I've traveled across 22 countries and most of the United States.

By day I'm a barber. And there is something sacred about that chair. People sit down a stranger and leave having told you things they haven't told their closest friends. Their marriages falling apart. Their dreams they've never said out loud. Their fears, their losses, their small wins. They trust you with their appearance, the thing the world sees first and somewhere in that vulnerability they end up trusting you with everything else too. I've been a counselor, a therapist, a life coach, and sometimes a doctor, all before noon. That kind of human connection doesn't stay in the shop. It travels with you.

And I won't lie, this blog is born out of necessity. At 34, life threw me a curveball I didn't see coming. A chapter closed in a way that hurt deeply. I turned 35 in February alone in a hotel room, waiting for a government letter to tell me where my life goes next.

As I write this I am in Longforgan, Scotland, staying in a hotel, waiting on a date that will send me back to Mexico and force me to start over. How did a California boy end up in Scotland in the first place? That's a story for another day. And why Mexico and not back to California where I was born? Let's just say home is more complicated than a zip code. I'll explain that one too, soon. What I can tell you is this: it's not the first time I've had to start from scratch. If I'm being honest it feels like the 28th time.

I had something good here, a barbering career that was growing, a life I was building, friendships I was making. Losing it hurts. The months of uncertainty, waiting on a decision from the Home Office, not knowing which way life was going to fall, took everything out of me. The stress and anxiety were so heavy I literally felt like my body was shutting down. I spent some holidays alone. My birthday too. Just me, a hotel room, and the silence of a life on pause.

This blog is for anyone who has ever felt stuck, scared, or too small for the life they imagined. You don't need to be scared. You just need to go.

I have no idea what's coming next. Then again, that's kind of the whole point. Follow along and figure it out with me.
